question: What does the systolic blood pressure reading actually measure?

options.C: Total volume of blood in circulation

explanation: Think of the top number (systolic) as the pressure in your arteries when your heart squeezes to push blood out to the body. You've got this! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the diastolic blood pressure measuring?

options.A: To calculate the maximum output of the left ventricle
options.B: To determine the strength of the heart valve closure
options.C: To measure arterial pressure during heart relaxation
options.D: To assess the velocity of blood inside the vena cava

explanation: The bottom number (diastolic) checks the pressure in your arteries while your heart takes a quick rest between beats. Great job keeping these straight! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h1)

question: Where are the body's main blood pressure sensors (baroreceptors) located?

options.B: Right atrium and superior vena cava

explanation: Baroreceptors hang out in the carotid sinuses (in your neck) and the aortic arch to keep a close eye on your blood pressure. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h2)

question: What is the main job of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)?

options.A: Rapid dilation of peripheral capillary beds
options.B: Direct stimulation of SA node pacemakers
options.C: Immediate reduction of heart rate during rest
options.D: Long-term control of blood volume and pressure

explanation: The RAAS acts like your body's long-term thermostat for fluid balance and blood pressure. You are mastering the basics! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h2)

question: Which blood pressure range is classified as Stage 1 hypertension?
explanation: Stage 1 hypertension starts when the top number is 130-139 or the bottom number is 80-89 mmHg. Keep practicing, you're doing great! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h3)

question: A patient's blood pressure is read at 185/115 mmHg. What urgent situation is this?
explanation: Any reading over 180/120 mmHg is a red flag and needs immediate medical attention to prevent organ damage. Stay sharp, future nurse! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h3)

question: What happens to a blood pressure reading if the cuff you use is too small?

options.A: It only affects the diastolic value
options.B: It has no effect on the measurement
options.C: It gives a falsely low reading
options.D: It gives a falsely high reading

explanation: A tight, small cuff squeezes the arm too hard, making the blood pressure look much higher than it actually is. Always pick the right cuff size! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h4)

question: A patient jogs into the clinic and immediately wants their blood pressure checked. What should you do?

options.A: Use a manual sphygmomanometer instead of a digital machine
options.B: Inflate the cuff twenty millimeters higher than usual
options.C: Allow the patient to rest for five minutes before measuring
options.D: Take the measurement immediately and document the reading

explanation: Exercise naturally boosts blood pressure! Letting them rest for about 5 minutes gives you an accurate, true-at-rest reading. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h4)

question: How is primary (essential) hypertension best described?

options.A: Transient pressure spikes triggered by acute stress
options.B: Blood pressure elevation caused by endocrine tumors
options.C: High blood pressure with no single identifiable cause
options.D: Elevated pressure caused directly by kidney failure

explanation: Primary hypertension develops slowly over time without one single clear medical trigger. You're building a solid clinical foundation! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h5)

question: Which of these is a classic cause of secondary hypertension?
explanation: When the renal arteries narrow (stenosis), the kidneys think the body has low blood pressure and trigger the RAAS, raising your BP. Excellent clinical recall! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h5)

question: Generally, what blood pressure reading is considered hypotension (low blood pressure)?
explanation: Readings dropping below 90/60 mmHg are typically flagged as hypotension. You're doing awesome! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the key sign of orthostatic hypotension?

options.A: Chronic low pressure only occurring while sleeping
options.B: A drop in blood pressure when changing positions
options.C: High blood pressure triggered by high sodium intake
options.D: Spikes in pressure caused by emotional anxiety

explanation: Orthostatic hypotension happens when your blood pressure dips suddenly as you stand up from sitting or lying down, making you feel dizzy. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which lifestyle change is known to help lower high blood pressure?
explanation: Cutting back on salt helps your body hold onto less water, which easily takes pressure off your blood vessels. Simple and effective! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why do doctors often prescribe diuretics for patients with high blood pressure?

options.A: To slow down the electrical conduction of the heart
options.B: To block the action of adrenaline on the heart
options.C: To dilate peripheral arteries by relaxing smooth muscle
options.D: To promote fluid excretion and reduce blood volume

explanation: Diuretics help your kidneys flush out extra salt and water, lowering the overall fluid volume in your pipes. You've got this pharmacology down! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why does long-term high blood pressure lead to left ventricular hypertrophy (thickening of the heart)?

options.A: Coronary arteries deliver too much oxygen to the tissue
options.B: Increased blood volume stretches the heart muscle walls
options.C: Valves in the heart become rigid and fail to close fully
options.D: The heart works harder against high arterial resistance

explanation: Just like lifting weights makes your arm muscles bigger, your heart muscle gets thicker from constantly pumping against high pressure in the arteries. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h8)

question: Which of these body parts is NOT a primary target for organ damage from chronic hypertension?
explanation: High blood pressure mainly damages delicate blood vessels in vital organs like the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes—not your everyday skeletal muscles. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h8)

question: Why is it so important to teach hypertensive patients to keep taking their medications even when they feel fine?

options.A: Blood pressure medications cure the underlying disease
options.B: Hypertension is typically an asymptomatic condition
options.C: Patients must adjust their doses daily based on mood
options.D: Stopping medication abruptly causes immediate heart failure

explanation: High blood pressure is called the 'silent killer' because it usually has no symptoms. Patients need to know the meds are working even when they feel completely normal! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h9)

question: A patient on a new blood pressure medication says they feel dizzy when standing up in the morning. What is your best advice?

options.A: Double the salt intake in the daily diet
options.C: Rise slowly from a sitting or lying position

explanation: Advise them to take their time getting out of bed! This gives their blood vessels a chance to catch up and prevents dizzy spells. Fantastic nursing intervention! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T6#GNS111_U2_T6_h9)
